title: Dual abelian varieties and the line-bundle homomorphism
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety]. The functor of invertible-sheaf families on $A\times_kT$ that are algebraically trivial on every geometric fibre and rigidified along the identity section (modulo isomorphism respecting the rigidification), is represented by an abelian variety $A^\vee$ of dimension $\dim A$, with universal Poincare sheaf $\mathcal P_A$ on $A\times_kA^\vee$. Here algebraic triviality means algebraic equivalence to the trivial sheaf; algebraic equivalence is the equivalence relation generated by two fibres of an invertible-sheaf family over a connected smooth parameter variety. The Poincare sheaf is normalized to be trivial on both identity axes. For an invertible sheaf $L$ on $A$ [def-sc-invertible-module], the family
$$L_0=m^*L\otimes p_1^*L^{-1}\otimes p_2^*L^{-1}$$
(on choosing the harmless constant-line normalization at $(0,0)$) represents a homomorphism $\phi_L:A\to A^\vee$ with $x\mapsto[t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1}]$, and $L_0\cong(1\times\phi_L)^*\mathcal P_A$. The maps $m,p_1,p_2$ are addition and the two projections; $t_x$ denotes translation by $x$. For every $b\in A(k)$, $\phi_{t_b^*L}=\phi_L$. For every homomorphism $a:B\to A$ of abelian varieties, pullback of families defines $a^\vee:A^\vee\to B^\vee$, and
$$\phi_{a^*L}=a^\vee\phi_La.$$
In particular $[-1]^\vee=[-1]$ and $\phi_{[-1]^*L}=\phi_L$. For an effective Cartier divisor $F$ on $A$, meaning a closed subscheme locally cut out by one non-zero-divisor [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle], the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O_A(F)$ is ample [def-sc-ample] if and only if $\phi_{\mathcal O_A(F)}$ is an isogeny, meaning a surjective homomorphism with finite scheme-theoretic kernel.

source.place: Chapter I §§5, 8, 9: theorem of the square; Proposition 8.1 and Remark 8.2 (effective line-bundle ampleness criterion); dual variety and Poincare universal property, pp.36–40, including Remark 8.7(e); §9 opening paragraph (dual homomorphism). Translation invariance and the pullback formula follow by substituting translations in the defining family.

proof.text: By [lem-sc-abelian-variety-projective] and [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization], $A$ is projective and geometrically integral. Apply [lem-sfb-projective-picard-identity-representability] with $X=A$ and $e=0$, and provisionally denote its proper connected identity component by $P$. It represents exactly the rigidified fibrewise algebraically trivial families in the statement, with tensor group law and universal sheaf $\mathcal P$. Both identity-axis normalizations are part of that representing construction. Smoothness and dimension of $P$ will be proved below; they are not assumed here.

source.place: I §8, universal property, printed pp.36–37; general projective Picard input as recorded in the auxiliary

proof.text: Let $c:A\times A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Use the explicitly normalized family $N_L=m^*L\otimes p_1^*L^{-1}\otimes p_2^*L^{-1}\otimes c^*(0^*L)$. Cancellation gives its canonical trivializations on both identity axes. Its fibre at $y$ is $t_y^*L\otimes L^{-1}$ up to a constant one-dimensional factor. These classes are algebraically trivial: the same family, parameterized by the connected smooth variety $A$, connects each fibre to the trivial fibre at $0$. Thus [lem-sfb-projective-picard-identity-representability] gives a unique $\phi_L:A\to P$ and $N_L\cong(1\times\phi_L)^*\mathcal P$. Dropping the constant factor after choosing a basis of $0^*L$ gives the displayed $L_0$ in the item.

source.place: I §8, construction using L*, printed pp.39–40

proof.text: Apply [thm-sc-theorem-of-cube] on $A_x\times A_y\times A_z$. Rearranging its seven factors, and retaining the constant identity-line factors, gives $N_L(x,y+z)\cong N_L(x,y)\otimes N_L(x,z)$ as families on the first factor, rigidified at $x=0$. For example the unnormalized quotient of these two sides is $L_{x+y+z}L_xL_yL_z/(L_{x+y}L_{x+z}L_{y+z})$, which is trivial by the cited cube identity; the identity-line normalization cancels its remaining constant factor. Representability and the tensor group law identify this equality of families with $\phi_L(y+z)=\phi_L(y)+\phi_L(z)$. The zero fibre gives $\phi_L(0)=0$, so this is a homomorphism of group schemes.

source.place: I Theorem 5.5 and Remark 5.6, printed p.23; I §8 L*

proof.text: For $b\in A(k)$, substitute $(x,y,b)$ in the same cube identity. It says, after cancelling $L_x,L_y,L_b$ and normalizing the two axes, that $N_{t_b^*L}\cong N_L$ as rigidified families on $A\times A$. Apply the uniqueness in [lem-sfb-projective-picard-identity-representability] to obtain $\phi_{t_b^*L}=\phi_L$. This is an equality of morphisms, since the cube was used on the whole parameter scheme, rather than just on its rational points.

Apply the same representing construction to $B$. Pulling a rigidified family back by $a\times1$ preserves its rigidification because $a(0)=0$, and preserves algebraic equivalence by pulling back each family in its defining chain. It also preserves tensor products. Hence it defines a homomorphism $a^\vee:P_A\to P_B$. For a variable $y\in B$, $a\circ t_y=t_{a(y)}\circ a$, so $(a\times1)^*N_L$ evaluated at $a(y)$ is the normalized family $t_y^*a^*L\otimes(a^*L)^{-1}$. This equality of pullback families over $B$ gives $\phi_{a^*L}=a^\vee\phi_La$ by representability.

source.place: I §9, opening paragraph, printed p.41; substitution in normalized families

proof.text: For the universal algebraically trivial line bundle $M$ on $A\times P$, its translated difference is again algebraically trivial on each fibre, by the connected family used in step 2. Thus it defines $d:A\times P\to P$, $(x,[M])\mapsto[t_x^*M\otimes M^{-1}]$. On $A\times\{0\}$ it is zero. Apply [lem-sc-rigidity] with first factor $A$, connected second factor $P$, and separated finite-type target $P$. The first factor is proper, geometrically connected and geometrically reduced by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]. Rigidity makes $d$ independent of $x$, and $d(0,[M])=0$ makes it identically zero. By the representing property the normalized family $N_M$ is trivial, universally over $P$. Pulling the resulting identity $m^*M\cong p_1^*M\otimes p_2^*M$ back by $x\mapsto(x,-x)$ shows $[-1]^*M\cong M^{-1}$, with identity normalization. Consequently $[-1]^\vee=[-1]$ on $P$. Step 5 and the homomorphism property now give $\phi_{[-1]^*L}=(-1)\phi_L(-1)=\phi_L$.

source.place: I Proposition 8.4 and Remark 8.5; scheme-family proof via rigidity

proof.text: Suppose $H$ is ample and put $K=\ker\phi_H$. This is a closed subgroup: it is the inverse image of the closed identity of the separated group $P$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-closed-subgroup-reduced-component], $B=(K_{\mathrm{red}})^0$ is an abelian subvariety and $\dim B=\dim K$. Since $\phi_H|_B=0$, the representing identity for $N_H$ restricts trivially on $B\times B$. Pulling back along $(1,-1):B\to B\times B$ shows $H|_B\otimes[-1]^*(H|_B)$ is trivial up to a constant line. The restriction $H|_B$ is ample. Let $H^{\otimes m}$ be very ample [def-sc-ample]; restricting its closed immersion $A\to\mathbf P^N$ to $B$ gives a closed immersion $i:B\to\mathbf P^N$ with $i^*\mathcal O(1)\cong M:=H^{\otimes m}|_B$, defined by the restricted sections $s_0,\dots,s_N\in H^0(B,M)$, which generate $M$. The complete linear system $j:B\to\mathbf P(H^0(B,M)^\vee)$ satisfies $i=\pi\circ j$, where $\pi$ is the linear projection dual to $k^{N+1}\to H^0(B,M)$, defined on the open complement of the common zero locus of the $s_k$, which contains $j(B)$. Hence $j$ is a monomorphism; it is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated], hence a closed immersion by [lem-pc-proper-monomorphism-closed], so $M$ is very ample. Its inverse pullback is ample too, and [lem-sc-ample-tensor] makes their tensor product ample. On a positive-dimensional proper geometrically integral $B$, a trivial bundle cannot be ample: [lem-pc-h0-proper-variety] gives $H^0(B,\mathcal O_B)=k$, so every morphism defined by sections of a trivial power is constant and cannot be a closed immersion. Hence $\dim B=0$, and the closed-subgroup auxiliary makes $K$ finite, including its possible infinitesimal structure.

source.place: I Proposition 8.1, printed p.35 (ample implies finite kernel)

proof.text: Choose an ample $H$ using [lem-sc-abelian-variety-projective]. The map $\phi_H:A\to P$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] and has finite kernel by step 7. For a closed target point its residue field is $k$ by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base]. Every nonempty fibre has a closed point by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], again rational over $k$. Choose one, $u$; then $v\mapsto v-u$ and $w\mapsto u+w$ identify that entire scheme-theoretic fibre with the finite kernel. Empty fibres cause no problem. The positive-dimensional-fibre locus is closed by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fibre-dimension-upper-semicontinuous]; if nonempty, Jacobson density would give a closed target point in it, which we just ruled out. Thus all fibres have dimension at most zero, and [lem-zl-finite-type-fibre-image-dimension-bounds] gives $g\leq\dim P$. The Picard tangent identity [lem-sfb-projective-picard-identity-representability] and [lem-sfb-abelian-structure-h1-dimension] give $\dim_kT_0P=g$. By [lem-ag-group-identity-local-dimension] and [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-cotangent-dimension], $\dim P\leq g$. Equality follows, and the same local-ring criterion makes $\mathcal O_{P,0}$ regular.

source.place: I Remark 8.7(e), printed p.37; dimension and regularity argument filling the scheme-theoretic gap

proof.text: The regular closed-point smoothness criterion [lem-weil-pbc-regular-closed-point-smooth-source] on an affine neighborhood of $0$ makes $P$ smooth at $0$. Every closed point is $k$-rational by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], so translation gives the same local-ring regularity and smoothness at every closed point. The smooth locus is open (it is the union of the neighborhoods on which the affine-local smooth condition holds). Its closed complement, if nonempty, contains a closed point by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], a contradiction. Thus $P$ is smooth everywhere. It is already proper and connected, so it is the abelian variety $A^\vee$ required in the statement, and step 8 proves $\dim A^\vee=g$. Apply [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization] to see that it is irreducible as well.

source.place: I §8, dual variety and Remark 8.7(e); local-ring smoothness verification

proof.text: Any $\phi_L$ with finite scheme-theoretic kernel is surjective now that $A$ and $A^\vee$ have equal dimension. Indeed the closed-target fibres are translates of the kernel, and the proper fibre-dimension and Jacobson argument of step 8 makes every fibre zero-dimensional. By [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] the homomorphism is proper, and its image $Z$ is closed by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-closed-image]; Since $A$ is reduced, its map factors through $Z_{\mathrm{red}}$: on affine opens, functions vanishing on the image pull back into every prime ideal and hence to zero. The fibres of this factorization agree with the fibres already considered. Apply [lem-zl-finite-type-fibre-image-dimension-bounds] to this finite-type map with $d=\dim Z$ and $n=0$ to get $g\leq\dim Z$; the image inequality for $A\to A^\vee$ gives $\dim Z\leq g$. A proper closed subset of the irreducible $g$-dimensional $A^\vee$ has dimension less than $g$: any chain in that closed subset can be extended by the irreducible whole space. Hence $Z=A^\vee$. In particular, step 7 makes $\phi_H$ an isogeny for every ample $H$.

source.place: I §8, printed p.40 (isogeny associated with an ample bundle)

proof.text: For the converse let $L=\mathcal O_A(F)$ with $F$ effective and suppose $\ker\phi_L$ finite. Let $D=F_{\mathrm{red}}$ as a reduced closed subscheme and $S=\operatorname{Stab}_A(D)$, which exists by [lem-sfb-closed-translation-stabilizer]. The group $C=(S_{\mathrm{red}})^0$ is an abelian subvariety by [lem-sfb-abelian-closed-subgroup-reduced-component]. The Cartier-divisor clause of the stabilizer auxiliary gives $\mu^*F=p_1^*F$ on $A\times C$. Consequently $\mu^*L\cong p_1^*L$; restricting this isomorphism along $0\times C$ identifies $L|_C$ with the constant line $0^*L$, so the normalized family $N_L|_{A\times C}$ is trivial. Representability gives $\phi_L|_C=0$. The closed immersion $C\to A$ therefore factors through the finite scheme-theoretic kernel; hence $\dim C=0$. The closed-subgroup auxiliary now makes $S$ finite.

source.place: I Proposition 8.1, omitted converse; auxiliary stabilizer argument, using Milne Algebraic Groups Corollary 1.81

proof.text: Steps 2–3, proved using [thm-sc-theorem-of-cube], identify $[t_a^*L\otimes L^{-1}]$ with $\phi_L(a)$ and make $\phi_L$ additive. Thus the class of $t_a^*L\otimes t_b^*L\otimes t_{-a-b}^*L\otimes L^{-\otimes3}$ is $\phi_L(a)+\phi_L(b)+\phi_L(-a-b)=0$, so by the representing property of [lem-sfb-projective-picard-identity-representability] (over $T=\operatorname{Spec}k$) that sheaf is trivial up to a constant line. Over $k$ any constant line is trivial, so $t_a^*L\otimes t_b^*L\otimes t_{-a-b}^*L\cong L^{\otimes3}$. Thus the sum of the three translated effective divisors is a member of $|L^{\otimes3}|$. Given $x\in A(k)$, first choose $a$ so $t_a^*F$ does not contain $x$. Then choose $b$ avoiding the two proper translated supports that would make $t_b^*F$ or $t_{-a-b}^*F$ contain $x$. Each choice is possible because $A$ is irreducible by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]. Every nonempty avoiding open in the smooth variety $A$ has a $k$-point by [lem-pc-rational-points-dense]. This proves that $L^{\otimes3}$ is generated by global sections: for any point choose a closed specialization using [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space]; a section nonvanishing at that specialization also does not vanish at the original point, since its nonvanishing locus is open. The same argument applies when $F=0$; then the translated divisors are empty. By [lem-fin-proper-coherent-finite-dimensional], $V=H^0(A,L^{\otimes3})$ is finite dimensional. The quotient $V\otimes\mathcal O_A\twoheadrightarrow L^{\otimes3}$ gives $f:A\to\mathbf P(V)$ and $f^*\mathcal O(1)\cong L^{\otimes3}$ by [lem-trf-projective-bundle-quotient-geometry].

source.place: I §6, proof of Theorem 6.4, printed p.30: triple translates; applied to Proposition 8.1 converse

proof.text: If $x,y\in A(k)$ have $y-x\notin S(k)$, some translate of $D$ contains $x$ but not $y$. To see this, the parameters of translates through $x$ and through $y$ are respectively $D-x$ and $D-y$ (since $x\in t_a^*D$ means $x+a\in D$). If the first were contained in the second, translation would inject the finite set of its irreducible divisorial components into the same set: containment between these components of equal dimension is equality. The injection is a permutation, so the two reduced supports would be equal. Equality would mean $y-x\in S(k)$. The resulting nonempty difference is an open subset of a reduced component and contains a $k$-point by Jacobson density and the closed-point residue-field lemma. Fix such a translate $t_a^*F$. Choose $b$ with neither $t_b^*F$ nor $t_{-a-b}^*F$ passing through $y$, by avoiding two proper closed sets. The section with zero divisor their sum vanishes at $x$ and not at $y$, so $f(x)\ne f(y)$. Fix a closed target point $z$. Its residue field is $k$ by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], so the closed points of $A_z$ are $k$-points of $A$. If $A_z$ is nonempty, choose one such point $x$ by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space]. The separation just proved forces every closed point of $A_z$ into the finite coset $x+S(k)$. Thus $A_z$ has finitely many closed points, and [lem-sc-positive-dimensional-locally-algebraic-closed-points] rules out a positive-dimensional irreducible component. Empty fibres already have dimension $-\infty$. The morphism $f$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated], since its source is proper and its target separated. By [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fibre-dimension-upper-semicontinuous], the set of target points whose fibres have positive dimension is closed. If nonempty it contains a closed point by [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], contrary to the preceding calculation. Thus every fibre has dimension at most zero.

source.place: I §6, proof of Theorem 6.4; point separation modulo the support stabilizer for I Proposition 8.1 converse

proof.text: The morphism $f$ is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated]. Its fibres are Noetherian and zero-dimensional by step 13, so [lem-sc-zero-dim-noetherian-finite-discrete] makes them finite discrete spaces. Since $f$ is of finite type and quasi-compact, [pqf-lem-qf-finitefibres] makes it quasi-finite; [cor-pqf-proper-quasifinite-finite] now makes it finite. A finite morphism is affine by [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Since $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P(V)}(1)$ is ample, [lem-weil-pbc-pullback-ample-invertible] makes $L^{\otimes3}=f^*\mathcal O(1)$ ample in the absolute sense. The projective-space twist is very ample, hence ample; its standard affine nonvanishing charts verify the absolute sense directly. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ample-very-ample-immersion-affine-base] to obtain an immersion from a positive power of $L^{\otimes3}$. This immersion is proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] and is a monomorphism, so [lem-pc-proper-monomorphism-closed] makes it closed; the projection argument of step 7 then makes the complete linear system of that power a closed immersion as well. Thus $L$ is ample in the definition [def-sc-ample]. Combining this converse with steps 7 and 10 gives the effective Cartier divisor criterion, with finite scheme-theoretic kernel and surjectivity exactly as stated.
